config_normalisation.definition: the config's own per-dimension mean and std, applied before any metric is taken, so every quantity here lives in the space the model predicts in

citations.text: assert np.all(scale > 0), "a state dimension is constant over the training episodes"

nrmse_scale.definition: the standard deviation of config-normalised state dimension d, taken over the rows belonging to TRAINING episodes only
properties: computed ONCE and stored; never recomputed per timestep
never derived from held-out data, so the metric's denominator carries no information about the arena it is scored on
strictly positive by assertion, so the metric cannot go non-finite

coverage.aggregation: an unweighted mean over the flattened array; every triple carries equal weight, so a horizon-h figure is dominated by the deepest steps only in as much as they are more numerous, which they are not -- each step contributes equally
coverage.caution_seeds_are_not_trajectories: in task1_calibration.py the per-seed error and sigma arrays are concatenated along axis 0 before pooling, so seeds enter the coverage average as if they were extra trajectories. That is fine for a point estimate -- it is a mean of means over a balanced design -- but it is NOT a valid resampling unit. Every interval in this paper resamples whole trajectories; pooling seed x trajectory and resampling the pooled vector narrows intervals by about sqrt(3) (M-27).

citations.note: the coverage itself: cumulative over steps 1..h, flat mean over all axes
where seeds join the trajectory axis
the nominal it is judged against

coverage.cumulative_not_pointwise: IMPORTANT. cov(h) averages steps 1..h. It is not the coverage at step h. The same convention is used for the err/sigma ratio and for every horizon-indexed quantity in the paper.
coverage.definition_in_words: the fraction of scalar (trajectory, forecast step, state dimension) triples whose absolute realised error is at most k times the sigma predicted for that same triple
coverage.name: coverage at +-k sigma

nominal.why: z is built from an ABSOLUTE error, so z <= k is the two-sided event and the nominal is erf(k/sqrt(2)): 68.27% at k=1, 95.45% at k=2. The paper quotes these as 68.3% and 95.4%.

pooling_axes_in_order: axis 0: trajectory (and, where several seeds are scored together, seeds are CONCATENATED onto this same axis before pooling -- see the caution below)
axis 1: forecast step, taken cumulatively over steps 1..h so coverage at h is an average over the whole rollout up to h, not the value AT step h

which_sigma.aleatoric: the mean over ensemble members of each member's predicted per-dimension sigma (system_dynamics.py:125)
which_sigma.epistemic: the per-dimension standard deviation across members' mean predictions. NOTE the scalar the METHOD applies is this summed over dimensions (system_dynamics.py:126); for a per-dimension coverage the per-dimension form is the only one that types.

nrmse_form2.aggregation_form: form 2: divide per dimension, then average. A mean of ratios.

citations.text: """FORM 2, retained for continuity with everything reported before M-19."""

nrmse_form2.name: nRMSE (form 2) -- reported only for continuity
nrmse_form2.status: superseded as the primary aggregation by form 1 at Task 3d

nrmse_pooled.aggregation_form: form 1: POOL over dimensions, then divide. A ratio of means, not a mean of ratios.

citations.text: sqrt( mean over dims of MSE_d ) / mean over dims of scale_d

nrmse_pooled.name: nRMSE (form 1, pooled) -- THE PRIMARY AGGREGATION
nrmse_pooled.reading: 1.0 means no better than predicting the training mean; below 1.0 means the model carries information
nrmse_pooled.what_it_is: normalised RMSE with a denominator fixed once over the training episodes, so it cannot approach zero
nrmse_pooled.why_form_1: form 2 (mean over d of RMSE_d / scale_d) is a mean of ratios and gives whichever dimension has the smallest scale unbounded leverage. The choice between them once inverted a comparison against the released model (M-19, R-27, R-29). Form 2 is retained only for continuity with numbers reported before M-19.

overconfidence_factor.it_is_a_ratio_of_means: NOT a mean of ratios. mean|error| and mean sigma are each averaged over the same pooled axes first, and the ratio is taken once at the end. The mean-of-ratios form is unbounded whenever a single sigma is near zero, which is exactly the regime 5.3 puts these models in.
overconfidence_factor.name: overconfidence factor (mean |error| / mean sigma)
overconfidence_factor.reads_as: rho = 1 is not calibration -- a calibrated Gaussian has mean|error| / sigma = sqrt(2/pi) = 0.7979. rho is reported as a magnitude of miscalibration, and coverage is the calibrated reading. Both are given everywhere for that reason.
overconfidence_factor.what_it_is: the headline calibration number: how many times larger the typical realised error is than the typical predicted sigma

citations.note: the aggregate is a flat mean
the upstream line this reproduces, verbatim in behaviour

relative_l1.denominator: the TRUE state at the same timestep, summed over all 45 dimensions. It is recomputed at every timestep and is not a constant.
relative_l1.known_pathology: the denominator is a 45-term sum in normalised space and can pass through zero, which is why relative-L1 goes non-finite on low-dimensional state groups (M-09: `inf` on base angular velocity from h>=8, an 11.4% blow-up rate on projected gravity at h=368). This is the reason a second metric exists.
relative_l1.name: relative-L1
relative_l1.space: normalised state space: both numerator and denominator are in the config-normalised units, not physical units
relative_l1.start: t_0 = history_horizon = 32; the first 32 steps are teacher-forced and excluded from the metric
relative_l1.what_it_is: the reference metric, reproduced verbatim in behaviour so our numbers are comparable to the upstream's printed one

A_over_B_training_claim.why: it is the upstream's own metric; the claim is about reproducing the upstream's comparison

calibration_claims.metric: overconfidence factor and coverage at +-1 sigma
calibration_claims.why: a calibration claim is about sigma against realised error, and neither relative-L1 nor nRMSE involves sigma

ranking_claims.metric: Pearson r between the applied scalar penalty and total absolute error over a rollout
ranking_claims.why: a ranking claim is about order, not scale
